notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The layered production shape this note selects from — A practical guide to building agents (OpenAI, PDF)

  • Start at the simplest composition and add layers only from measured need — Building Effective AI Agents (Anthropic)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • agentic reference architecture — the seven layers, what each does, and how they wire together.

  • Components of an agentic system — the components as a vocabulary.

What this note adds: the whiteboard decision, not the blueprint. Forty-five minutes doesn't buy seven boxes, so this is the order you draw them in, the two that are non-negotiable on day one, and what each omission costs when the follow-up comes.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The two you never skip? Gateway (auth, limits, spend cap) and observability. Even for a toy.
Draw order? Loop → tools → gateway → observability → state → guardrails → router.
Which layer is skipped most and shouldn't be? Observability. Without traces you can't debug or eval anything.
Which is safe to defer? Model router — one model until cost or latency says otherwise.
What "name and skip" sounds like? "Guardrails sit here; I'd come back to them." Said, not drawn.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I don't draw seven boxes in a design round — I draw four and name the rest. The loop and the tool layer go up first because that's where the design actually lives, then the gateway and observability, because those two are non-negotiable even on day one: without the gateway there's no place to put a spend cap, and without tracing nothing is debuggable or evaluable. State, guardrails and the model router get named out loud with one sentence each on when I'd add them. Drawing all seven reads as a platform diagram copied from a blog post; drawing four and defending the omissions reads as someone who has shipped one.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Minimum viable — loop + tools + gateway + observability Day one of anything real, and the default opening in a round. No durability, no guardrails, one model. Long runs and safety come later. Single agent, single tenant, runs measured in seconds.
Add state Runs can be interrupted, resumed, or paused for a human. A store, a serialisation format, and a schema you now have to version. Runs over ~30s, or any approval step.
Add guardrails as a layer Untrusted input reaches the loop, or actions are consequential. A policy surface to own, plus latency on the checked path. Multi-tenant, regulated, or user-supplied content in context.
Full seven, including model router Cost or latency has been measured and one model isn't serving both. Routing logic, per-model evals, and a fallback matrix to maintain. You can state the cost or latency number the router is fixing.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you add Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Gateway One entry point holding auth, rate limits, and the spend cap. Where per-run and per-tenant caps get enforced — not in the prompt. Tenant-level throttling and a place to shed load.
Observability A span per step and per tool call, with tokens and cost attached. Storage for traces; trivial next to what it saves. Everything else becomes measurable — evals, cost attribution, debugging.
State / checkpointer A durable store keyed by thread; makes resume and HITL possible. One write per step. Buys back the cost of re-running failed long runs. Checkpoint size and schema migrations become your problem.
Guardrails Input, output and action rails outside the model, as a policy engine. Latency per checked call; a second model call if a classifier is involved. Rejection rate per rail becomes a signal — and a tuning burden.
Model router A selection step before each call, plus a fallback path per provider. The point of it: cheap model for routing and extraction, frontier for planning. Per-model evals, and a matrix of which failures fall back where.

The redraw test: each of these is a box you can point at. If adding a layer to your answer doesn't add a box or a store to the picture, you named a concern rather than a component.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Why the gateway is non-negotiable. It's the only place a spend cap can be enforced, because every other candidate is inside the thing being capped. A cap in the prompt is a request the model can ignore; a cap in the loop is code that a runaway loop is already failing to reach. At the gateway it's a counter checked before dispatch, which is the one position that survives the failure it exists to contain.

Why observability is the other one. Every metric from §1 — task success, cost per successful task, steps per task, p95 — is computed from traces. Skipping the tracing layer doesn't just cost debuggability; it makes the entire metric set unmeasurable, which means you cannot tell whether any later change helped. It is the cheapest layer to add and the most expensive to retrofit, because the runs you most want to understand are the ones that already happened.

The order, justified by dependency rather than taste. State depends on nothing; guardrails depend on there being a tool boundary to enforce at; the router depends on having cost or latency numbers, which depend on observability. So observability precedes the router by necessity, not preference — routing without per-step cost data is guessing which calls to downgrade.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The rule underneath it: draw what the brief forces, name what it doesn't. Each omission gets one sentence saying the trigger that would bring it back — "no router yet; I'd add one when planning and extraction diverge on cost" — which converts a gap into a deliberate choice and usually invites the follow-up you want.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "We can't tell why it's expensive. Finance has a number and we can't attribute it to anything."

Root cause. The team had shipped an agent with loop, tools and a gateway, and deferred observability as a "phase two" item because the agent worked and traces felt like tooling rather than product. Cost was visible only as a monthly provider invoice. With no span per step there was no step count, no per-tool attribution, and no way to tell an expensive run from a cheap one — so the first optimisation attempt was guesswork, and a model downgrade that saved tokens quietly cut task success with nothing to measure the trade against.

Fix. Tracing went in, and within a week the picture was obvious: one tool was being called repeatedly inside the loop because its error message didn't tell the model what was wrong. The retrofit cost was small in code and large in lost time, because the months of runs that would have shown the pattern had not been recorded. Observability is the layer whose value is entirely in already having it.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

You drew four boxes. Isn't the reference architecture seven?

It is, and I'd name all seven — but drawing all seven in a design round tells you nothing about my judgement, because it's the same picture for every brief. What I'm doing is showing which ones this problem forces and which I'd defer, since that's the part that differs between a support agent and a research agent.

The two I never defer are the gateway and observability. Everything else is a response to something in the brief: durability because runs are long, guardrails because input is untrusted, a router because a cost number says so.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Guardrails deferred sounds risky. Why is that not the wrong call?

Because "guardrails as a layer" and "no controls" are different things. The tool-layer boundary is in the minimum viable set — typed arguments, scoped credentials, validation in code — and that's what stops the common failures. A guardrails layer is the addition of a separate policy engine: input classification, output filtering, a rules surface someone maintains.

I defer the layer when the input is trusted and the actions are reversible, because a policy engine with nothing consequential to protect is cost and latency for a governance story. What flips it is untrusted content reaching the loop — at that point injection is the threat and a boundary alone isn't enough.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

At ten teams on one platform, which layer becomes the bottleneck first?

The gateway, and not for throughput reasons — for policy. It's the single place holding auth, rate limits and spend caps, so every team's requirements land on it, and it becomes a config surface nobody owns. The failure looks like a team shipping without a spend cap because the gateway's defaults didn't cover their shape.

The fix is to make the gateway's policy declarative and per-tenant rather than a shared config, so onboarding a team means adding a record rather than editing shared code. The second pressure is observability, where the problem is schema rather than volume — if teams emit different span attributes you can't compare cost per successful task across them, which is the main thing a platform should be able to answer.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the layering so a simple agent and a complex one share infrastructure.

I'd make the layers independently adoptable rather than a stack you buy whole. Gateway and observability are mandatory and provided — you can't deploy without them, and they need no configuration to be useful. State, guardrails and routing are opt-in, each behind an interface that a simple agent simply doesn't reference.

The design constraint that matters is that adopting a layer later must not be a rewrite. So the loop talks to the tool layer through one interface whether or not a guardrail sits behind it, and state is written through a store abstraction that starts as an in-memory implementation. That way "add durability" is a config change and a backing store, not a refactor of the agent.

What I'd resist is a framework that requires all seven from the start. It makes the simple agent carry the complex one's concepts, and the usual outcome is teams routing around the platform to ship something small — after which you have the layering and the shadow implementations.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "Draw the full reference architecture — it shows you know the production shape."

✅ Reality: It shows you can reproduce a diagram. The signal is which boxes this brief forces and which you'd defer, with the trigger for each. A seven-box answer to a simple brief reads as over-engineering, which is the failure mode interviewers probe for.

❌ Trap: "Observability is tooling — we'll add it once the agent works."

✅ Reality: Every metric you'd use to define "works" is computed from traces. Without it you cannot measure task success, cost per success, or steps per task, so you cannot tell whether any later change helped. It's cheap to add and impossible to backdate.

❌ Trap: "The gateway is just an API layer — nginx does it."

✅ Reality: For agents it's the enforcement point for spend caps and per-tenant concurrency, which is a semantic job, not a proxy one. It's the only position outside the loop, so it's the only place a cap survives a runaway loop.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • agentic reference architecture — the blueprint this note selects from.

  • deployment and scaling — what the gateway and worker layers do under load.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §2 Where authority to act lives — the tool layer is one of the four you always draw.

  • §10 Spend caps in the gateway — that decision needs this layer to exist.

  • §12 Tracing is a requirement — observability being non-optional is this note's claim.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Internal agent platform — the Tier 4 answer is that problem's opening.

  • §14 "Our agent succeeds 60% and costs too much" — usually starts with a missing observability layer.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Guides and sensors — the harness controls split, and why most quality lives there — Harness engineering (Böckeler, martinfowler.com)

  • Tool and context design as the lever, ahead of model choice — Writing effective tools for agents (Anthropic)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Harness Engineering — Agent = Model + Harness — the framing, and the guides/sensors taxonomy.

  • Harness, loop & context engineering — the vocabulary map — which word means which part.

What this note adds: the budget consequence of the framing. If the harness is where the controllable quality lives, then "the model isn't good enough" is a claim that needs evidence — and this is how you get it before spending a sprint on the wrong half.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The split? Agent = model + harness: loop, tools, context assembly, checks, environment.
Which half do you control? The harness. The model is a dependency you swap, not a thing you fix.
How to tell which is failing? Classify failures from traces: planning, tool, context, or model.
The tell of a harness problem? A human with the same context and tools would have succeeded.
Cheapest harness fix, usually? Tool error messages the model can act on.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

When an agent underperforms, the question is whether to change the model or the harness, and the default answer is the harness — because that's the half I control and where most fixable quality sits. Before spending anything I classify a sample of failures from traces into planning, tool, context and model failures. Only the last is a model problem. In practice the biggest wins are usually tool contracts and error messages, because a tool that fails uninformatively turns a recoverable step into a loop. Upgrading the model is the fix when the classification says so, not the opening move.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Fix the tools Failures cluster on one tool, or the agent retries the same call. Contract work per tool, and a redeploy per change. Repeated identical calls; errors the model can't act on.
Fix the context The information was available but not in the window at the right step. Retrieval or assembly work; possibly a state redesign. The agent asks for something it was told earlier.
Fix the loop Drift, no termination, or steps that don't advance the plan. Usually a shape change — a graph instead of a free loop. Step count varies wildly on similar inputs.
Change the model Classification says the model had everything and still chose wrong. Re-run every eval; pin and re-validate; cost profile changes. A human with the same context and tools would have succeeded.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Tools Typed arguments, task-level operations, actionable error strings. Usually reduces steps, so it cuts cost while raising success. Per-tool failure rate becomes the thing you watch.
Context Adds assembly logic, retrieval, or a state promotion step. Can go either way — better selection often means fewer tokens. Window composition per step joins the trace.
Loop Replaces free iteration with a bounded graph and named terminations. Bounds the step count, which bounds both cost and p95. Failures start naming a node instead of "the agent".
Model Nothing structural — but pin the version and keep a fallback. Directly changes cost per step, in whichever direction. A full eval re-run, and a rollback plan for the swap.

The redraw test: three of the four change the picture. Swapping the model changes a config value — which is exactly why it's attractive, and exactly why it's rarely the highest-value fix.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The classification, which is the whole method. Take a sample of failed runs — fifty is usually enough to see the shape — and bucket each by the earliest step that went wrong:

  • Planning — the decomposition was wrong before any tool ran.
  • Tool — the call failed, or returned something the agent couldn't use.
  • Context — the needed fact existed but wasn't in the window at that step.
  • Model — everything was present and correct, and the choice was still wrong.

Only the last bucket is a model problem. In most first-generation agents it is the smallest, and the tool bucket is the largest — which is the entire argument of this note expressed as a count rather than an opinion.

Why tool errors are the highest-leverage fix. An uninformative error turns one failed step into several: the model retries, varies the arguments, retries again, and burns the step budget without progress. Because run cost grows with the square of step count, collapsing a four-attempt flail into one clean failure-and-recover is a disproportionate saving — and it's usually a string change.

The honest test before a model upgrade. Re-run the same failed traces against the candidate model with the harness unchanged. If success doesn't move, the harness was the constraint and the upgrade is buying you a higher bill. That experiment costs one eval run and settles an argument that otherwise consumes a sprint.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The last branch is the one people miss. If a competent human with the same context and tools would also have failed, the problem is neither model nor harness — the task is under-specified, and no amount of either will fix a goal the system can't tell it has achieved.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "We upgraded to the newest model and task success barely moved. It cost more and the team was out of ideas."

Root cause. The agent's search tool returned {"error": "bad request"} on any malformed query, with no indication of what was malformed. The model would retry with a slightly different phrasing, fail the same way, and burn most of its step budget before giving up. That pattern accounted for a large share of failed runs, and it was invisible without per-step traces because the run ended with a plausible partial answer rather than an error. A better model made the same retries slightly faster.

Fix. The tool's errors were rewritten to say what was wrong and what a valid call looked like — a change measured in lines, not days — and the retry behaviour collapsed to one corrected attempt. Task success moved substantially on the original model, which also settled the upgrade argument in the opposite direction from where it started.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

What exactly counts as the harness?

Everything around the model call that you wrote: the loop and its termination conditions, the tool definitions and their error messages, how the window is assembled each step, the checks run on output, and the environment the tools act in. The model is the one component you didn't write and can't modify.

That boundary is the useful part, because it separates what you can iterate on this week from what you can only swap and re-evaluate. Most "the model isn't good enough" conversations are really about the half nobody has examined.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

When is upgrading the model genuinely the right first move?

When the classification says the model bucket dominates, and specifically when failures are reasoning failures on complete information — the agent had the right context, called the right tools, got good results, and drew a wrong conclusion. That's not fixable with better plumbing.

The other legitimate case is a capability gap rather than a quality gap: the task needs long-context coherence, or reliable structured output, or tool-use behaviour the current model doesn't have at all. That's a different argument from "it makes mistakes", and it's worth saying which one you're making.

I'd still run the controlled test first, because it's cheap and it's the only thing that distinguishes the two.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

The model is a dependency you don't control. How does that change the design?

It means pinning and fallback are architectural, not operational details. I pin the model version, because a silent provider-side update can change behaviour in ways your evals catch only after the fact. And I keep a fallback path to at least one other provider, which forces the prompt and tool definitions not to depend on one vendor's quirks.

The deeper consequence is that evals become a standing cost rather than a launch activity. A dependency that changes without your involvement has to be re-validated on a schedule, and the eval set is the only thing that makes a version bump a decision rather than a leap. That's also what makes the harness investment compound — every harness improvement is yours permanently, while every model improvement is rented.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the process that decides where a team spends its next quality sprint.

I'd make failure classification a standing artifact rather than an investigation. Traces are already required, so the addition is a labelling step: every failed run gets bucketed, by a rubric applied by a judge with human spot-checks. That produces a weekly distribution across planning, tool, context and model.

The sprint then goes where the distribution points, and the rule is that a model change requires the controlled experiment first — same traces, new model, harness held constant. Without that rule the model bucket absorbs everything ambiguous, because upgrading is the easiest action to take.

What I'd watch over quarters is whether the distribution shifts. A healthy trajectory has the tool bucket shrinking as contracts mature and the model bucket becoming proportionally larger — at which point upgrading genuinely is the highest-value move, and you have the data to defend it.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "Quality is a model problem — we'll upgrade when the next one ships."

✅ Reality: The model is one component and the one you can't change. Most fixable quality is in the tools, the context and the loop. Classify failures before spending, or you'll pay more for the same behaviour.

❌ Trap: "Prompt engineering is the harness."

✅ Reality: The prompt is one input to context assembly. The harness is also tool contracts, error strings, loop bounds, and the checks between steps — and those are where the compounding wins are, because they change what the model can do rather than what it's asked to do.

❌ Trap: "A better model makes the harness matter less."

✅ Reality: It raises the floor and leaves the structure intact. A stronger model still can't recover from an error message that doesn't say what went wrong, and still pays the steps² cost of a loop with no bound. Harness defects survive upgrades.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Harness Engineering — Agent = Model + Harness — the framing this note budgets against.

  • Tool error handling — why error strings are the leverage point.

  • the architects framing — debugging by classification.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §4 Tools are an API contract — the usual destination of a harness sprint.

  • §12 Tracing is a requirement — classification is impossible without it.

  • §13 Version prompts, tools, model and graph together — the pinning this note argues for.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 "Our agent succeeds 60% and costs too much" — this note is the first move in that problem.

  • §14 Coding agent — tool feedback quality is the dominant variable there.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Never trust model output as an authorisation decision — the agency argument — OWASP LLM06: Excessive Agency

  • Validate at the boundary; the tool layer as the enforcement point — A practical guide to building agents (OpenAI, PDF)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • agentic reference architecture — the seven layers and how they wire together.

  • excessive agency — the threat when an agent can act beyond its mandate.

  • permissions and least privilege — scoped credentials and the confused-deputy problem.

What this note adds: the architectural seam those notes assume — that deciding and acting are different layers with different trust levels — and what moves in the diagram when you put the boundary in the wrong place. The security notes own the threat; this one owns where the line is drawn.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The one-line rule? The loop decides, the tool layer acts. Authority never lives in the loop.
Why can't the loop hold authority? Its input is untrusted — tool results and retrieved docs carry injected instructions.
What is the boundary concretely? Argument validation, scope check and policy, in code, before any effect.
Cheapest violation to spot? A tool that takes a raw SQL string, shell command or URL from the model.
What the model's output actually is? A request to act, not a decision to act.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I keep authority out of the loop. The model decides what it wants to do and the tool layer decides whether that's allowed — argument validation, scope checks and policy all live in code on the other side of the boundary. The reason is that the loop's input is untrusted: tool results and retrieved documents can carry instructions, so anything the model emits is a request, never an authorisation. The tell that a design gets this wrong is a tool that accepts a raw command string, because then the tool layer has no contract to enforce and authority has silently moved into the model.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Authority in the loop — model output executes directly Prototypes and internal demos with no real side effects and no untrusted input. Any injected instruction becomes an action. There is no enforcement point to add later without a rewrite. Tools take free-form strings; the "safety" is prompt wording.
Authority in the tool layer — model proposes, code authorises The default for anything with real effects. Every tool needs a typed contract and a validation path; adding a tool is now real work. Tools are task-level with JSON Schema; effects run behind checks.
Split by direction — reads free, writes gated Large read surface, small write surface — the common production shape. Two policy paths to keep straight; a read tool that leaks data is easy to under-police. The tool list is mostly retrieval with a handful of mutations.
Authority in a separate policy service Multi-tenant platform, many tools, compliance requirements. A network hop per action and a service to run; over-engineering for one agent. Several teams share tools, and policy has to be audited centrally.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
In the loop No boundary box at all — the loop touches the world directly. Cheapest to build, and the cost arrives later as an incident. Nothing to monitor at the boundary, because there isn't one.
In the tool layer A validation/authorisation box between loop and effects; per-tool scoped credentials hang off it. Small per-call overhead; the real cost is contract work per tool. You monitor rejected calls — a rising rejection rate is drift or injection.
Split by direction One path straight through for reads, one through policy for writes; idempotency keys on the write path. Writes carry the gate latency; reads stay fast, so p95 depends on the mix. Two dashboards. The read path needs its own egress/data-exfil watch.
Policy service A dedicated box outside the agent, called per action, with its own audit store. A network hop per action — meaningful when actions are frequent. Policy becomes a deployable artifact with its own versioning and rollback.

The redraw test: in every option except the first there is a box between the loop and the world. If your diagram has the loop drawing arrows straight into databases and APIs, you've chosen option one whether you meant to or not.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The blast-radius arithmetic. This fork has no benchmark; what settles it is counting what a single injected instruction can reach. For a given design:

reachable_effects = Σ (tools callable by the loop without a check)

An agent with twelve tools where nine are reads and three are unchecked writes has a blast radius of three — and the question to ask out loud is what the worst of those three does. If the answer is "sends email to a customer" or "issues a refund", the fork is already resolved.

The one number worth quoting. OWASP lists Excessive Agency as a top-ten LLM risk precisely because the impact scales with the permissions granted rather than with the model's error rate. That framing is the argument against "the model is accurate enough" — accuracy changes how often you reach the bad action, and permissions change what the bad action does.

The measurement to run. Audit the tool graph for paths to an irreversible effect and count the ones that pass no check. It's a static analysis over the registry, the number should be zero, and it grows silently every time someone adds a tool — which is why it belongs in CI, not a design review.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The questions, in order:

  1. Does this tool change anything outside the process? If yes, it is on the authority side of the line by definition, no matter how harmless it looks.

  2. Can I type its arguments? If the tool takes a raw query, command or URL, gating it is theatre — the check has nothing to check. Redesign it to a task-level operation with typed parameters first.

  3. Who is it acting as? The credential must be scoped to the end user, not to the agent's own service account. An agent holding broad credentials is the confused deputy, and no amount of validation at the boundary fixes it.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "A support ticket contained instructions, and the agent followed them."

Root cause. The agent had a run_query tool that accepted a SQL string, because that was the fastest way to give it access to the data it needed. A customer pasted text into a ticket that read as instructions to the model, the retrieved ticket body entered the context as tool output, and the loop emitted a query it had been told to emit. There was no boundary to stop it: the tool layer's contract was "a string", so validation had nothing to validate, and authority had in effect moved into the model the moment that tool was designed.

Fix. The free-form query tool was replaced by three task-level tools with typed parameters and a read-only role, which made the injected instruction unexpressible rather than merely disallowed. The lesson that generalises is that this was a tool design failure rather than a prompt failure — no system-prompt wording would have held, because the tool granted the capability directly.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

You keep saying the tool layer authorises. What does that actually mean in code?

It means the call from the loop lands on a function that validates arguments against a schema, resolves the credential for the acting user, checks the action against policy, and only then performs the effect. The model's JSON is an input to that function, never a substitute for it.

The practical consequence is that a tool is an API with a contract, not a passthrough. If I can't write down what a valid call looks like, I can't enforce anything — which is why the design work lands in the tool signature rather than in the prompt.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Doesn't that boundary slow you down? Every new tool is now a whole contract.

It does, and that friction is the point — it's what keeps the blast radius proportional to deliberate decisions rather than to how fast someone was moving. The place I'd spend to reduce the friction is tooling: a registry where a tool declares its schema, scope and rung once, so adding a tool is filling in a form rather than inventing a policy.

Where I'd accept the cost without complaint is the write path. Reads can be made cheap with a shared scoping helper, but anything that mutates state earns its contract, because that's where a mistake is expensive to unwind.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

At fifty tools, the boundary is enforced per tool. What breaks?

Coverage stops being checkable by reading. At that size nobody can hold the policy in their head, so the failure mode moves from "this tool is wrong" to "there is a path I didn't know existed" — typically a generic tool like execute_code or call_webhook that reaches an effect the specific tools guard carefully.

So at scale the unit of audit becomes the tool graph rather than the tool. I'd generate the reachable-effects set in CI, fail the build when an unchecked path to an irreversible effect appears, and require a rung and scope on every new tool as a registry requirement rather than a review comment. The other break is credential sprawl, which argues for token exchange issuing short-lived scoped credentials per call rather than long-lived secrets per tool.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the tool layer for a platform where many teams publish tools into one agent.

I'd make the boundary a platform service rather than a library, because a library is advice and a service is enforcement. Teams publish a tool as a declaration — schema, scope, side-effect class, autonomy rung — and the platform generates the callable wrapper. The loop never gets a reference to a team's code directly.

Identity is the part I'd design first. Calls carry the end user's identity through token exchange, so a tool receives a short-lived credential scoped to that user and that action, which makes the confused-deputy problem structurally hard rather than a thing teams must remember. The audit record is emitted by the platform, not by the tool, so it exists whether or not a team bothered.

I'd watch rejection rate per tool and per tenant. A spike is either a prompt regression or an injection attempt, and both want the same response — sample the rejected calls. That signal exists only because the boundary is a real component.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "We tell the model in the system prompt not to take destructive actions without asking."

✅ Reality: A prompt is a request to a component whose input is attacker-influenced. Instructions arriving through tool results compete with yours on equal footing. The control has to be code on the other side of the boundary.

❌ Trap: "We validate the model's output, so we're safe."

✅ Reality: Validating shape isn't authorising intent. A well-formed call to refund(order_id, amount) passes schema validation perfectly while being the wrong action for this user. Validation is necessary; scope and policy are what authorise.

❌ Trap: "Read-only tools don't need a boundary."

✅ Reality: Reads are how data leaves. A read scoped to the agent rather than to the user is the confused deputy, and a read tool combined with any outbound call is the exfiltration half of the lethal trifecta. Reads need scoping even when they need no approval.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • agentic reference architecture — the layers this note draws a line between.

  • excessive agency — the threat model behind the rule.

  • permissions and least privilege — scoping, which is the other half of the boundary.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §4 Read tools vs write tools — this note's boundary is what makes that split enforceable.

  • §1 Autonomy level — the rung is a policy the tool layer applies; without the boundary there is nowhere to apply it.

  • §11 Indirect prompt injection — untrusted input in the loop is exactly why authority sits outside it.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — refunds are the canonical effect behind this boundary.

  • §14 Data / SQL analyst agent — the free-form-query failure story is this decision made wrongly.

  • §14 Internal agent platform — the Tier 4 answer is the platform version of this seam.

notes.title: Where the sync/async line falls, and what the client is promised

headings.text: ⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Durable execution and resumable runs — what the async side buys you — LangGraph: durable execution

  • Streaming partial results so a long run stays legible to the client — Anthropic API: streaming messages

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • deployment and scaling — why synchronous request/response breaks for agents, and the accept → enqueue → worker → poll shape.

  • streaming and real-time agents — how streaming is implemented.

What this note adds: where the line actually falls and what the client contract becomes on each side — #98 owns the async machinery, this owns the threshold and the promise you make to the caller.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Where is the line? ~30s p95. Past that, hold no connection — return a job id.
What actually sets it? Infrastructure timeouts you don't control: LB, proxy, browser, gateway.
What changes for the client? The response becomes a receipt, not an answer. Every caller must handle it.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I draw the line at roughly thirty seconds of p95, and the reason isn't the agent — it's everything between the client and it. Load balancers, proxies and API gateways idle out at values I don't control, so a run that might exceed that has to return a job id rather than an answer. The part people underestimate is that this is a client-contract decision, not a deployment one: once the response is a receipt, every caller needs a poll or a subscribe path, and retrofitting that across existing consumers is the expensive part.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Synchronous request/response p95 comfortably under the shortest timeout in the path — roughly 30s, often less. A slow run holds a connection; under load, connections exhaust before compute does. Bounded step count, no tool that waits on a human or a third party.
Sync with streaming Run is long-ish but the client is a UI that benefits from progress. Connection still held; reconnection and resume logic now belong to the client. A human is watching, and partial output is useful before the end.
Async: job id + poll Runs may exceed the timeout, or the caller is a backend. Two round trips minimum, and the client must own polling and backoff. Batch, scheduled, or server-to-server callers.
Async: job id + webhook/subscribe Long runs where the caller can receive a push. Delivery guarantees, retries and endpoint auth become yours to run. Runs of minutes to days, or a human approval pause in the middle.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Sync Gateway → runtime inline. No queue, no job store. Simplest. Concurrency is bounded by held connections, which is a low ceiling. Watch connection pool saturation; it exhausts before CPU does.
Sync + streaming Adds SSE/WebSocket transport and a resume-from-offset path. Same tokens, better perceived latency. Proxy buffering and idle timeouts become a real class of bug.
Async + poll Adds a queue, a job store, stateless workers, and a status endpoint. Queue and store are cheap; the cost is the poll traffic and the extra hop. Queue depth and job age become the health signals, not request latency.
Async + webhook Adds an outbox, delivery retries, signing, and consumer endpoint registration. Delivery infrastructure is a real line item. You now run a delivery system: dead letters, replay, consumer outages.

The redraw test: async puts a queue and a job store in the diagram and turns the gateway response into a 202. If your answer doesn't change the response code, you haven't crossed the line.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "It works locally and times out in staging at exactly sixty seconds, every time."

Root cause. The run averaged twenty seconds, so it had been built synchronously and tested that way. The p95 was closer to ninety once a retry or a slow tool landed, and the ALB in front of it had a sixty-second idle timeout nobody had looked at. Because the model streams nothing until it has something to say, the connection sat genuinely idle during long tool calls, so the timeout fired on exactly the runs that mattered most — the hard ones.

Fix. Short term, streaming heartbeat events kept the connection alive and bought headroom. Properly, the endpoint moved to accept-and-return-a-job-id with a status endpoint. The expensive part wasn't the queue — it was that three internal callers had been written against a synchronous contract and all of them had to change, which is the cost of discovering the line late rather than choosing it early.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • deployment and scaling — the async execution shape this note chooses between.

  • streaming and real-time agents — the streaming half of the fork.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §7 Durable execution — async runs must survive a worker crash, which makes checkpointing mandatory rather than optional.

  • §7 HITL as a durable pause — a human gate forces the async side of this fork regardless of run length.

  • §9 Stream progress, not just tokens — what the client sees while the run is open.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Deep research agent — minutes-long runs, so async plus progress streaming is the only shape.

  • §14 Voice / interview agent — the opposite end: sub-second turns make async a non-starter.

notes.title: Who owns the flow — your code or the model

headings.text: ⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The model as one step inside code you wrote, rather than the owner of the flow — Building Effective AI Agents (Anthropic)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Agents-vs-Workflows — predefined code paths versus model-directed control.

  • State Machines & Explicit Control Flow for Reliability — bounded loops and named terminations.

What this note adds: the per-step version of the ladder decision. Which rung picks the shape for the whole task; this asks, inside a shape you've already chosen, which individual steps still belong to deterministic code — because the answer is usually "more of them than you think".

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The rule? The model does judgement; code does everything with a right answer.
Cheapest step to reclaim? Routing on a value the code can already read.
Why it matters? Each reclaimed step removes a call, its tokens, and its failure probability.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Even inside an agent, most steps don't need a model. My rule is that the model handles judgement — ambiguity, language, ranking by taste — and deterministic code handles anything with a defined right answer: validation, arithmetic, routing on a known field, formatting, lookups. Every step I reclaim removes a model call, its tokens, its latency and its failure probability from the compounding chain. The version that goes wrong is an agent that asks the model to decide whether a date is in the past, which is a function call dressed as reasoning.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Code owns the step There's a defined right answer: parse, validate, compute, route on a field. Rigidity — the code handles what you anticipated and nothing else. You could write the assertion for it.
Model owns the step The step requires judgement over ambiguous or natural-language input. A call, its tokens, and one more term in p^N. Two reasonable people could answer differently.
Model proposes, code decides Judgement is needed but the outcome must be constrained. Both costs — but the failure is bounded to a known set. Classification into fixed categories; extraction into a schema.
Code with a model fallback The common case is deterministic and the tail isn't. Two paths to maintain and test. A parser that handles 95% and gives up on the rest.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Code A function in the graph, not a node that calls a model. Removes a call entirely — tokens, latency and a failure term. Testable. Failures are exceptions with stack traces.
Model A model call with its own prompt, retries and output handling. One call per invocation; re-bills the accumulated context. Non-deterministic; needs an eval to know it still works.
Propose + decide A model call plus a validator that maps output to an allowed set. Model cost, but failures degrade to a default instead of propagating. Watch the rejection rate — it's a drift signal.
Code + fallback A deterministic path plus a model path behind a condition. Pays for the model only on the tail, which is where the value is. Fallback rate is the health metric; a rise means the parser rotted.

The redraw test: reclaiming steps for code makes the diagram smaller, which is the one improvement that never shows up in a feature list.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "It occasionally mis-sorts results, and we can't reproduce it."

Root cause. A retrieval agent asked the model to rank candidate documents by recency after retrieval, as part of a larger reasoning step. Dates were present on every candidate, so the ordering had a single correct answer — but it was being produced by a language model along with several other judgements in one call, and occasionally the ordering came back subtly wrong. Nothing failed; the output was well-formed and plausible, and the bug surfaced only as quiet quality variance no one could reproduce on demand.

Fix. Sorting moved into code, and the model's step was narrowed to the part that genuinely needed judgement — deciding which documents were relevant. The general lesson is that bundling a deterministic operation into a reasoning step makes it non-deterministic, and you lose the ability to assert on it. If you can write the test, write the function.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Agents-vs-Workflows — the ownership question at task scale.

  • Structured Output & Constrained Decoding — how "propose, then decide" is enforced.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §1 Which rung of the ladder — this is the same fork applied per step rather than per task.

  • §8 Compounding error — every reclaimed step removes a term from p^N.

  • §10 Model routing — a step that must stay with a model may still not need the frontier one.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Data / SQL analyst agent — schema lookups and validation are code; the ambiguity is the model's.

  • §14 Back-office workflow automation — the whole value is reclaiming steps for deterministic code.

notes.title: Managed agent runtime or your own
notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • A managed runtime's scope — session state, identity, observability, durability — Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • build vs buy — the full build-vs-buy analysis and what each platform provides.

What this note adds: the one-line placement — which layers a managed runtime actually replaces, and the lock-in that matters is the state model, not the SDK.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What a managed runtime replaces? Gateway, state, scaling, identity, tracing — not the loop or your tools.
The lock-in that bites? The state and memory model, not the SDK surface.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

A managed runtime buys the infrastructure layers — session state, autoscaling, identity, tracing, durability — and leaves the loop and the tool contracts to you, which is where the design lives anyway. So it's a good trade for a small team shipping one agent. The lock-in that matters isn't the SDK, which is usually thin; it's the state and memory model, because that's what your agent's behaviour comes to depend on and what has no portable equivalent. I'd adopt one to get to production, and keep tools behind my own interfaces so the expensive half stays mine.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Managed runtime (Bedrock AgentCore, Vertex Agent Engine) Small team, one or two agents, standard shape, cloud already chosen. Their state model, their limits, their release cadence. You're rebuilding queues, sessions and tracing from scratch.
Framework on your infra (LangGraph, Agents SDK) You want the orchestration primitives but own deployment. You still run the platform — scaling, durability, tenancy. Custom control flow, existing infrastructure to reuse.
Own runtime Many teams, unusual requirements, or tenancy the platforms don't model. Everything a platform gives you, built and staffed. You are the platform team, and agents are the product.
